Use this subject or life material: moderating an online forum for amateur astronomers.

Aim for about 437 words.

I had always viewed the night sky as a sanctuary of quiet wonder, a perspective that naturally led me to join CosmicLens, a thriving online forum for amateur astronomers. When I was invited to serve as a community moderator at sixteen, I imagined my duties would primarily involve organizing monthly photo contests, cataloging deep-sky targets, and answering beginner questions about telescope focal lengths. Instead, I quickly learned that even a hobby dedicated to the vast, serene cosmos is not immune to the chaotic friction of human ego and conflicting perspectives.

The real test arrived during a bitter forum-wide schism between purist visual observers and modern astrophotographers. What began as a technical debate over digital image enhancement swiftly devolved into elitist gatekeeping, personal insults, and aggressive thread-hijacking. Unprepared for such hostility, I initially relied on rigid enforcement, locking active threads and deleting contentious comments without warning. Rather than restoring peace, my heavy-handed censorship fueled accusations of administrative bias, deepened the toxicity, and alienated long-time contributors, pushing our once-vibrant digital observatory to the brink of a permanent fracture.

Watching the community crumble under my management made me realize that my approach to leadership was fundamentally flawed. I had treated moderation as an exercise in policing rather than facilitation. I recognized that the underlying issue was not a lack of rules, but a complete breakdown in empathy; both factions were fiercely passionate, yet each felt their unique way of experiencing astronomy was being invalidated. I needed to shift my strategy from top-down suppression to active mediation, transforming defensive arguments into constructive dialogue.

To mend the divide, I hosted an open virtual town hall where members could voice their frustrations directly without fear of instant deletion. Working alongside the moderation team, I restructured the forum architecture to create dedicated spaces for specialized techniques while launching a collaborative initiative that paired digital imagers with visual loggers for joint observation projects. By replacing arbitrary authority with empathetic structure, the animosity gradually subsided, and the forum transformed back into a supportive environment where differing methodologies were celebrated as complementary lenses on the universe.

Navigating this digital crisis taught me that harmony rarely comes from imposing silence, but from cultivating mutual respect through active engagement. The setback stripped away my naive assumptions about leadership, showing me that managing any community requires patience, active listening, and the flexibility to bridge disparate perspectives. Whether analyzing complex datasets in a research laboratory or navigating diverse group dynamics in a college seminar, I will carry forward the knowledge that bringing people together under a shared passion requires as much deliberate calibration as aligning the delicate optics of a telescope.

Use this subject or life material: working as a scribe for a blind student.

Aim for about 546 words.

Return only the essay text, with no title or commentary.

I signed up to be a scribe for a blind student named Idris because a sign-up sheet was taped to the counseling office door and I had a free period, and I want to be honest that my first reason for doing it was almost that thin. I did not know Idris. I knew he sat two rows over in AP Biology with a braille display and a cane folded under his desk, and that he laughed loudly at things that were not always funny, which I later learned was on purpose, a way of making a room comfortable with him before it had the chance to be awkward.

Being a scribe meant reading exam questions aloud and writing down his answers exactly as he said them, word for word, no editing, no fixing. It sounds simple. For the first few tests it was simple, mostly multiple choice, mostly quiet rooms. Then came the AP Bio free-response section in May, ninety minutes, three long questions about cellular respiration and gene expression, the kind of exam where a wrong transcription could cost real points on something he actually understood.

I got tired around the second question. That's the plain truth of it. I'd read for over an hour, my voice going dry, and when he started dictating his answer about the electron transport chain, he used the phrase "proton gradient" and I wrote "proton gradient," and later, when he corrected a sentence and asked me to change "increases" to "decreases" two lines up, I found the wrong line. I fixed the wrong sentence. He asked me to read it back to confirm, the way he always did, and I read back what I'd written, which was correct in the spot I'd changed and now wrong in the spot I hadn't touched, because in swapping the word I'd apparently also cut the original clause that made the sentence make sense at all.

He caught it. Of course he caught it - it's his own reasoning, and even without seeing the page he could hear that what I read back didn't sound like something he'd said. We fixed it together, slowly, with four minutes left on the section, both of us more rattled than we let on. He got the score he needed. I only found out weeks later, when the results came back, that it had been close.

What I think about is not the mistake itself so much as the ten seconds before he caught it, when I read the sentence back and thought it sounded fine. I had gotten comfortable enough in the role to stop double-checking my own hearing, to trust the fatigue in my own head over the precision his work actually required, and comfort turned out to be exactly the wrong thing to feel in that chair. Being part of that arrangement, week after week, had made me feel like I belonged to something - his exams, his effort, the strange tight community of just the two of us and a proctor at the back of the room - and belonging made me careless in a way that a stranger might not have been.

I still scribe for him. He never brought the free-response mistake up again, which somehow makes me think about it more, not less. I check every line twice now, out loud, before I let either of us move on.

Use this subject or life material: the neighbourhood basketball court that was demolished.

Aim for about 585 words.

Return only the essay text, with no title or commentary.

They tore down the court on Bellmore Street in June, the one with the crooked rim that made every shot bank in from the left whether you meant it to or not, the one where I learned to play and later taught my younger cousin to play, replaced almost overnight by chain-link fencing and a permit notice zip-tied to the post where the backboard used to hang.

I went to the city council meeting that August mostly to be angry in public, honestly, expecting a room of bored adults and a five-minute public comment slot where I'd say my piece about a lost neighborhood landmark and go home having accomplished nothing except venting. I did not expect to sit through the entire two-hour meeting, but I did, because somewhere around the second agenda item, listening to a planning official explain the actual zoning process that had turned that court into a future six-unit building, something shifted in how I was listening.

I had walked in assuming the decision was some faceless act of neglect, a court nobody valued being erased by nobody in particular. What I heard instead was a genuinely complicated, almost fascinating account of density requirements, a housing shortage the city had been tracking for a decade, a parcel that had technically been zoned for redevelopment since before I was born, and a public comment period two years earlier that almost nobody from our block had shown up to, myself included, because none of us had known to look for it. My anger didn't fully disappear. It changed shape, though, from something aimed at an anonymous "they" into something closer to real curiosity about how these decisions actually get made, who gets a say, and why the people most affected are so often the last ones paying attention.

That's the moment I'd point to if I had to name one - sitting in a folding chair in a municipal building at nine at night, watching a zoning map projected on a screen, realizing I had spent seventeen years walking past decisions like this one without any idea they were decisions at all, made by real people in rooms exactly like this, following rules I'd never bothered to read. I went home and looked up our city's zoning code that same night and read for almost three hours, well past when I meant to stop, cross-referencing parcel numbers against a map until I understood roughly how our whole neighborhood had been carved up decades before any of us moved in.

I still don't know if I think the condo building is a bad idea. Some nights I do, mostly when I miss the specific sound the old rim made. Other nights I think about how badly this city needs housing and I'm not sure a basketball court, however beloved, should automatically win that argument. What I do know is that I now read city council agendas the way some people read box scores, and I've started going to the meetings regularly, not to be angry anymore but because I actually want to understand what's coming before the fence goes up around it.

I turn to the planning official from that first meeting now, a woman named Ms. Okonkwo who answers my emails patiently and let me shadow her for a day in the fall, and to the zoning code itself, dense and badly formatted, which I somehow now find more absorbing than most of my actual homework. I never got the court back. I got something else instead, a way of seeing the neighborhood that I don't think I can unsee now, for better or worse.

Use this subject or life material: a grandmother's dementia.

Aim for about 669 words.

Return only the essay text, with no title or commentary.

My grandmother has a laminated card by her front door. It is A5, printed in eighteen-point Arial, and it says: THE DOOR IS LOCKED. YOU LOCKED IT. THE KEY IS IN YOUR LEFT COAT POCKET. Underneath, in a different font because we ran out of ink and reprinted the bottom half, it says: IT IS TUESDAY. NAOMI COMES ON THURSDAY.

I made it. I laminated it in the school library on the machine you have to ask for at the desk, and the woman there asked if it was for a project, and I said yes because the true answer was too long.

The card is the third version. The first one just said the thing about the key. The second added the day. The third added my name, because in November she rang my mother at eleven at night to ask who the girl who comes on Thursdays is, and my mother put the phone down and cried in the kitchen and I stood in the doorway holding a glass of water like an idiot.

Vascular dementia is not the kind where everything goes at once. It is the kind that goes in steps. She will be entirely herself for six weeks - sharp, funny, unkind about the neighbours in a way I find delightful - and then something drops, and it does not come back, and then she is stable at the new level for a while. So the card gets longer. Each line on it is a small stone marking where something used to be.

I have thought a lot about the physics of that card, which sounds like a strange thing to say. When I made the first one I thought of it as a note. A message from us to her. But it does not work like a message, because a message assumes a person who receives it and remembers receiving it. What the card actually is, I think, is a piece of her mind that we built outside her head and screwed to the wall. The knowledge that the door is locked used to live in her. Now it lives on the wall, and she goes to the wall to get it, the way you would go to a shelf.

That reframed something for me. I had been thinking of her as diminishing - as a smaller and smaller version of the person she was. But nobody keeps everything inside themselves. I do not know my own phone number without looking. I know approximately eleven facts and outsource the rest to a device in my pocket. The difference between her and me is one of degree and of dignity: I chose my prostheses and hers were chosen for her, by us, and put in eighteen-point Arial by a granddaughter who could not think of anything else to do.

The Thursdays are the good part and I want to be accurate about them rather than sentimental. Sometimes she knows me. Sometimes she thinks I am my mother at nineteen, which is not distressing for either of us, and I have stopped correcting it because correcting it helps nobody except my sense of being an honest person. We do the same things: we do the shopping list, we water the spider plant that is enormous and possibly indestructible, and she tells me about a dance in 1961 at the Locarno in Sheffield where a man called Vincent stood on her foot. She has told me about Vincent perhaps forty times and the details do not change, which the consultant says is normal: that memory is stored differently from the one about Tuesday.

I know things about my grandmother that my mother does not know, purely because I have heard the Vincent story forty times and my mother heard it twice in 1988 and stopped listening. That is what repetition gives you if you let it. The fortieth telling has details in it that the second one did not.

The card is getting full. I have been thinking about what happens when there is not, and whether we make a second card, and whether a wall of laminated A5 is a kind of person or a kind of loss, and I do not have an answer, but I keep noticing that I have started thinking about memory as something built rather than something possessed.

She is not diminishing. She is being redistributed - into a card, into a spider plant, into a girl who will be able to tell you exactly what Vincent did at the Locarno in 1961 long after there is nobody left who was there.

The heavy cast-iron skeleton of the 1952 Singer sat on the scarred wooden table, its inner gears locked in a stubborn silence. For the women at the community tailoring co-operative, this machine was not merely a tool; it was a lifeline, the sole mechanism capable of stitching the thick denim they sold to support their families. I had arrived that afternoon with little more than a screwdriver and a head full of YouTube tutorials, hoping to offer some volunteer labor. When I finally cleared the bird's nest of tangled thread and applied the last drop of oil to the shuttle hook, the needle began to dance with a rhythmic, steady hum. The room erupted in soft cheers, but it was the quiet gesture of the lead tailor, Elena, that caught me off guard. She walked over, pressed a small, worn piece of scrap fabric embroidered with a simple floral pattern into my palm, and bowed her head in a gesture of profound respect.

That scrap of fabric felt impossibly heavy in my hand, carrying the weight of a livelihood restored. I had expected a polite thank you, perhaps a glass of tea, but I had not prepared for the gravity of being treated as a peer whose skills held tangible value. Seeing their collective relief, I realized that my technical tinkering had become an act of preservation for their agency. This moment of gratitude did not just make me happy; it fundamentally shifted my perspective on the relationship between mechanical expertise and human dignity.

I returned to the co-operative every Saturday for months, eventually teaching the younger apprentices how to diagnose tension issues and timing errors themselves. The gratitude I felt for that initial interaction fueled a new motivation: to become a conduit for self-sufficiency rather than a temporary fix. My work transitioned from repairing machines to building confidence, as I realized that fixing a gear was secondary to ensuring these women could remain independent artisans.

This experience redefined my academic ambitions. I am no longer interested in engineering as a sterile, abstract discipline, but as a bridge between complex systems and human necessity. I want to study mechanical engineering to better understand how design choices impact the autonomy of those who depend on them.

The gift of that floral scrap remains pinned to my desk. It serves as a constant reminder that the most significant innovations are those that empower others to keep moving forward. Whenever I face a difficult problem, I recall that rhythmic hum of the Singer, and I am motivated to create solutions that honor the people they serve.

Instead, I received the final surviving fragments of Boorish, a regional dialect spoken by only four living relatives scattered across three continents. Growing up, I had occasionally heard snatches of this melodic language at family gatherings, dismissing it as affectionate nonsense or secret-keeping. Aunt Elena, however, approaching her ninetieth birthday and facing the quiet erasure of her generation, entrusted me with the responsibility of keeping their linguistic past alive. This unexpected gesture overwhelmed me with a profound gratitude that fundamentally shifted my perspective on identity, history, and my own place within a vanishing lineage.

That initial spark of thankfulness quickly evolved into an urgent sense of purpose. Realizing that I was holding the literal last bridge to an unwritten culture, I transformed myself from a passive relative into an active archivist. I began spending my weekends conducting frantic video calls with my great-aunt and three surviving elderly cousins, recording hours of colloquial stories, folk songs, and idiomatic expressions that existed nowhere else in the world. As I painstakingly transcribed these audio files, mapping dying vowels to modern phonetic charts, the gratitude I felt for Aunt Elena's gift blossomed into a deep motivation to study linguistics and cultural anthropology. The task was daunting, requiring patience and resilience, but every preserved phrase felt like a victory against the inevitable tide of forgetting.

This project taught me that gratitude is not merely a passive emotion of appreciation, but an active catalyst for stewardship. Documenting Boorish demanded a rigorous dedication that bled over into my academic life, teaching me how to approach complex problems with meticulous care and profound empathy. I began to see language not just as a tool for communication, but as a living vessel of human experience, carrying the humor, sorrows, and resilience of people who had survived immense historical displacement. The unexpected act of receiving a notebook sparked a lifelong commitment to preserving endangered cultural histories, ensuring that vulnerable voices do not slip silently into the dark.

Today, my ambition to pursue linguistics in college is directly rooted in those kitchen-table recordings and late-night transcription sessions. I want to dedicate my career to field documentation, stepping into the spaces where languages are fading to capture them before they disappear entirely. Aunt Elena passed away last winter, taking with her the last fluent cadence of her childhood, but her voice lives on in the digital archives I compiled and in the passion she inadvertently ignited within me. 

Ultimately, the greatest gift I received was not the linguistic data itself, but the realization of how much we stand to lose when we stop listening to one another. That gratitude has become my compass, guiding my academic pursuits and my desire to connect the fragmented pieces of human history. By ensuring that four voices are never forgotten, I found my own voice and a clear direction for my future.

Midnight at the twenty-four-hour pharmacy on the edge of the city was a crucible where the chaotic daytime world stripped away to reveal a stark, fluorescent-lit reality. As a night shift technician, I quickly learned that the hours between midnight and eight in the morning belonged to the vulnerable. The daytime pharmacy hummed with impatient professionals and rushed parents, but the night shift was different. It brought a steady stream of insomniacs, exhausted caregivers, and people grappling with sudden medical emergencies or chronic pain in the quiet dark. My job was simple on paper: count pills, enter prescriptions, and hand them across the counter. Yet, standing behind that register forced me to confront a side of humanity I had previously only read about in textbooks or glimpsed behind closed doors.

Initially, I approached the role through the detached lens of an efficient technician aiming for speed and accuracy. I viewed the endless rows of stock bottles and computer queues as logistical puzzles to be solved. However, this clinical detachment fractured the night a frantic father pounded on our security glass at two in the morning, holding an infant struggling to breathe because his insurance had inexplicably dropped his daughter's crucial nebulizer medication. While the system was locked and the corporate protocols demanded endless verification codes, the human element demanded immediate action. Instead of hiding behind policy, I stepped closer, listened to his cracked voice, and worked with the pharmacist to override the system and provide the medication immediately. Watching the sheer relief wash over his face made me realize that behind every digital profile in our database was a person enduring a deeply personal crisis.

That night fundamentally shifted my understanding of empathy, transforming it from a passive emotion into an active, operational necessity. I began to see that the prescription bottles we dispensed were not merely chemical compounds, but lifelines holding fragile routines together. I learned to read the subtle cues of exhaustion in the elderly woman picking up her husband's heart medication, and I recognized the quiet desperation in the young man refilling his anxiety treatment. Instead of rushing them through the transaction, I started offering a lingering presence, a patient ear, or a reassuring nod. I realized that my value as a worker was not measured solely by my processing speed, but by my capacity to hold space for others during their darkest hours.

Working the night shift also sparked a profound internal realization about my own resilience and capacity for growth. The isolation of the graveyard shift required a mental stamina I did not know I possessed, teaching me how to stay calm and grounded when the environment around me felt unpredictable and heavy. I discovered a quiet strength in myself, born not from grand achievements, but from the cumulative weight of small, unseen acts of kindness performed under fluorescent lights while the rest of the world slept. This experience tore down my sheltered worldview, replacing naive idealism with a grounded, compassionate awareness of the struggles others face daily. I emerged from those long, sleepless nights with a mature sense of purpose, recognizing that true personal growth begins the moment we look past our own convenience and genuinely connect with the struggles of the people standing right in front of us.

The fluorescent hum of the ceiling fan in my family's kirana shop serves as the steady metronome for my afternoons. While the streets outside blur into a cacophony of horns and heat, I am tucked behind the scratched wooden counter, surrounded by the scent of roasted cumin and laundry detergent. My task is simple yet hypnotic: keeping the accounts. To most, this is a monotonous chore of ledgers and receipts, but to me, it is a complex, living mosaic of our neighborhood's existence. Watching the columns of numbers align provides a strange, grounding satisfaction that makes the hours evaporate into the shelves of stacked dal packets and sugar bags.

This obsession stems from the realization that every entry in our weathered ledger tells a profound story. A sudden spike in flour sales at dawn signifies a community festival, while a quiet Thursday evening spent tracking the fluctuating price of onions offers a lesson in global logistics and local scarcity. I am fascinated by the patterns inherent in our daily transactions, finding beauty in the way consumption mirrors the rhythms of the lives around us. Each customer who approaches the counter is a variable in an equation I am constantly refining, a delicate balance of credit, trust, and mutual survival that sustains our modest livelihood.

When I seek to understand these patterns beyond the ledger, I turn to my grandfather. He is the repository of our shop's history, having spent four decades memorizing the purchasing habits of three generations of neighbors. Sitting with him, I trade my notebook for his anecdotes, learning how historical inflation rates once reshaped the way he stocked the aisles. He explains the nuance of seasonal credit - the unspoken social contract between the shopkeeper and the struggling family - which adds a layer of human depth to the stark mathematics I record. His stories transform my columns of ink into a narrative of community resilience.

Beyond these conversations, I immerse myself in introductory economics textbooks and online lectures, eager to map the formal theories I encounter against the micro-reality of our counter. I find a thrill in bridging the gap between grand macroeconomic principles and the tangible realities of a small retail operation. It is empowering to see how the demand curves I read about in class manifest in the specific requests of our regulars, proving that the world of commerce is not abstract or detached, but rooted in the very floorboards beneath my feet.

Maintaining these accounts has taught me that true focus is found in the intersection of numbers and empathy. I have discovered that my curiosity is not merely for bookkeeping, but for the intricate, interconnected systems that hold our society together. In the quiet solitude of the shop, I am not just tracking profits; I am participating in the steady pulse of human connection, one transaction at a time.

The basement smelled of wet drywall and ruin, a pungent mixture of mildew and defeat that clung to the back of my throat. My grandfather's darkroom, once a sanctuary of amber light and chemical alchemy, had been reduced to a waterlogged graveyard after a massive pipe burst. I stood in the doorway, paralyzed by the sight of ruined photographic paper and bloated cabinetry, feeling the crushing weight of lost history. I had spent years learning the art of silver gelatin printing within those walls, and watching the space decompose felt like losing a part of my own identity. I was ready to walk away, convinced that the damage was irreversible and the machinery permanently seized by the rising tide.

Then, my neighbor, an elderly retired engineer named Arthur, showed up with a heavy-duty shop vacuum and a box of hand tools. He did not offer empty platitudes or tell me it would be alright; instead, he simply began to pull apart the ruined floorboards. For three weeks, he showed up every morning at dawn, his knuckles scarred and his patience inexhaustible. He taught me how to stabilize the structural beams, re-wire the enlargers that had been shorted by the flood, and calibrate the ventilation system until the air finally tasted clean again. He never asked for payment or recognition, simply finding joy in the mechanical puzzle of restoration and the quiet companionship of our shared labor.

This act of unexpected generosity transformed my perspective on what it means to be part of a community. I had always viewed the darkroom as a solitary retreat, a place to hide away with my negatives and silence. Arthur's involvement taught me that the most meaningful things in life are often sustained by the hands of others. By investing his time into a project that offered him no tangible benefit, he demonstrated that gratitude is not a passive emotion but a call to action. His diligence became the bridge between my despair and my eventual recovery, showing me that destruction is rarely the end of a story if someone is willing to help you build it back up.

The restoration motivated me to seek out similar ways to contribute to the lives of those around me. I began volunteering at a local youth center, offering workshops on film photography to students who had never held a camera. I wanted to pay forward the grace Arthur had shown me, realizing that mentorship and labor are the most potent currencies we possess. This cycle of gratitude has shaped my approach to education; I now understand that my academic journey is not just about personal achievement, but about how I can stabilize the environments and people around me.

Today, when I step into that darkroom, I do not just see prints hanging from a line. I see the history of a pipe burst and the enduring kindness of a neighbor who refused to let me quit. This experience serves as a permanent reminder that our greatest obstacles are often the precursors to our deepest connections. I am fueled by the knowledge that we are built to support one another, and I carry that responsibility into every room I enter, eager to help others mend whatever has been broken in their own lives.

The battered shoebox under my bed contains the physical weight of a decade. Inside, bundled with twine and smelling faintly of cedar and dry ink, are fifty-two letters from a boy named Elias in a small village in rural Greece. When we first began our correspondence in middle school, the exchange was purely academic, a sterile exercise in cross-cultural curiosity. I was captivated by the exoticism of his Mediterranean life, while he meticulously questioned me about the glossy, fast-paced world of American suburbia. We were two strangers playing at friendship through the slow, deliberate medium of international airmail, never imagining how these sheets of paper would eventually map the topography of my own evolving identity.

As we grew older, the tone of our letters shifted from geographical descriptions to philosophical inquiries. My teenage preoccupations with grades and social hierarchies began to feel remarkably trivial when contrasted with Elias's reflections on his family's agricultural legacy and the encroaching pressures of a modernizing economy. I found myself agonizing over my responses, moving away from the superficial to the profound. I realized that my world was not the baseline of normalcy I had assumed it to be, but merely one version of existence among many. This correspondence acted as a mirror; by attempting to explain my life to someone so far removed, I was forced to articulate my own values and confront the biases I had internalized.

One particular winter, Elias wrote about the beauty of silence in his village, a stark contrast to the constant noise of my digital life. His words sparked a period of intentional reflection that led me to step back from the performative nature of my extracurriculars. I began to understand that connection is not built on the volume of our interactions, but on the depth of our vulnerability. Through our written dialogue, I learned to listen - truly listen - to the unspoken anxieties and aspirations that define the human condition, regardless of one's longitude or latitude.

This realization transformed my approach to my community. I transitioned from a passive participant in my high school environment to an active observer of human experience. I began seeking out voices that challenged my perspective, fostering conversations that required patience rather than soundbites. The act of waiting weeks for a reply taught me that the most meaningful growth often occurs in the spaces between moments of action.

Today, my relationship with Elias remains one of the most significant pillars of my life. He is no longer an exotic study, but a confidant who has witnessed my maturation from a distance. Through our letters, I have discovered that my identity is not a static destination, but a fluid journey shaped by the empathy we offer others. I carry these lessons into my future, ready to engage with the world not just as a resident of my own country, but as a global citizen committed to the slow, rewarding work of true understanding.

My grandmother used to grow chillies in Guwahati, on a strip of land behind the house she left when she moved here to live with us, and she talks about that garden more than she talks about almost anything else from her old life. Two years ago, for her seventy-fourth birthday, I decided I was going to grow her a full crop of chillies on our apartment balcony as a surprise, ready by the time she came back from a month visiting my uncle. I had never grown anything in my life. I figured how hard could it actually be, and that confidence is basically the whole story of what went wrong.

I bought six pots, some Kashmiri chilli seeds and some bird's eye seeds I found online because I wanted variety, and I started them in March, giving myself what I thought was plenty of time. I watered them every single day without fail, which I now know was the first real mistake, because chilli plants apparently prefer to dry out somewhat between waterings, and what I was doing was slowly drowning the roots while feeling proud of my consistency. I also used regular potting soil from the hardware store instead of anything with proper drainage, so the water had nowhere to go, and by May the leaves on four of the six plants had started curling and yellowing in a way I assumed, at the time, meant they needed more water, so I gave them more.

By the time my grandmother came home, two plants were dead outright and the other four were struggling, pale and stunted, with maybe a dozen small green chillies between all of them combined, nothing like the abundant, almost aggressive growth she'd described from her own garden. I hadn't told her about the project beforehand, so the surprise I revealed on the balcony that first evening was six sad pots that I had to explain were supposed to be a birthday gift, three months in the making, that had mostly failed.

She didn't laugh at me, though I think a part of me expected her to. She walked along the pots, picked up a handful of the soil, let it fall through her fingers, and said, quietly, that I'd drowned them, the way you'd say it about a fact rather than a failing. Then she asked why I hadn't asked her for help in the first place, since she'd grown these exact plants for probably fifty years before I was even born. I didn't have a good answer. I think I wanted it to be entirely mine, some kind of gift that didn't need her input to work, which is a strange thing to want when the whole point of the gift was to remind her of something she already knew everything about.

We replanted that same week, together this time, in terracotta pots with drainage holes she picked out herself, watering on a schedule she set based on how the soil actually felt rather than a fixed daily habit. The second attempt worked. We had chillies by August, not a huge crop, but real ones, and she used a handful of them in a curry that I thought tasted almost exactly like what she'd described from Guwahati, though I have no real way of knowing that for certain.

I still think about the six dead pots more than I think about the ones that survived. Not because the eventual chillies didn't matter, but because the failure taught me something the success never could have: that wanting to give someone a piece of their own life back requires actually asking them how it worked, not assuming I could reconstruct it out of confidence and an internet search. I got that wrong first. I don't think I'll get it wrong that particular way again.

The decision didn't come suddenly, though my brother tried to argue that it had. My father had been quieter for the past year, staying up later looking at the accounting books, talking to my mother in low voices about rent and staffing costs and how much the delivery platforms were taking. The restaurant was still doing okay, still had regular customers, still had a purpose in the community. He thought they should fight harder to keep it alive. I remember him saying, "Dad's just burned out. If he took a month off, he'd feel differently about this."

I think my brother was wrong, and I've been angry at him for not seeing it, which is probably why I'm writing about this instead of just moving on.

He'd been there at four in the morning to start prep. He'd listened to customers' problems and their stories and their complaints. He'd watched food trends change and rent increase and his own back and knees start to give out from standing all day. My brother wanted my father to keep sacrificing himself for something that was also sacrificing him.

So I downloaded a Python tutorial and decided I would build her something in a fortnight, because I had assumed that programming was a matter of knowing the right words, and that once you knew them you typed and things happened.

The fortnight became four months. I want to be honest that most of that time I did not enjoy it. I found it humiliating in a way I had not been prepared for. I am the kind of student who is used to being competent quickly, and here was a thing that would refuse to run because of a colon. Not a wrong idea - a colon.

The frog game was, by October, a rectangle that could jump. I showed Ines on a video call and she said, where is the frog, and I said it is being a rectangle at the moment, and she said, oh.

Here is where I changed my mind, and it happened at about eleven at night in November over something small.

I was trying to make the frog fall back down after jumping, and I had written it so that every frame the frog moved down by three pixels. It looked wrong. It looked like the frog was being lowered on a string. I could see it was wrong and I could not say why. And then - I genuinely remember the physical feeling of this - I thought about my mechanics homework, and the fact that falling things do not have a constant speed, they have a constant acceleration. So instead of moving the frog down three, I made a number called velocity, and each frame I added a bit to the velocity, and then moved the frog down by the velocity.

It took two lines. And the frog fell like a real thing falls.

I sat there for a while. What had happened was not that I had learned a coding trick. What had happened was that a piece of physics I had been able to recite for two years - that gravity is an acceleration, not a speed - had for the first time been something I could see. I had written the sentence "a = 9.81" perhaps two hundred times. I had never once believed it in my body until a green rectangle fell correctly off a ledge on my laptop.

That reorganised what I thought I was doing. Until then I had understood code as instructions: a way of getting a machine to perform tasks. From that night I understood it as a way of building a small claim about how something works and then watching whether the claim behaves. If your model of falling is wrong, the frog looks wrong. The screen is not judging your typing. It is judging your understanding.

After that I stopped being humiliated by the errors, mostly, because I had a different relationship with them. An error meant my model was incomplete, which is interesting, rather than that I was slow, which is not.

I decided, in the fall of eighth grade, that I was going to stop speaking Tagalog at home. Nobody told me to. My parents never once asked me to, and my grandmother, who lived with us and spoke almost no English at all, certainly never asked me to. I decided it on my own, in the particular quiet way that thirteen-year-olds decide things that will matter more than they understand, sitting in the back of a classroom where a boy had mimicked my mother's accent at pickup the week before, not cruelly exactly, just carelessly, the way kids repeat things without weighing them.

I told myself it was about efficiency. English was faster for me by then, more natural, and switching between languages mid-sentence felt like static I didn't want to deal with anymore. That was the story I gave myself, anyway. The truer story is that I had started to associate the sound of my first language with being marked as different, and I wanted, badly, to stop being marked.

So I answered my mother in English when she spoke to me in Tagalog. I answered my grandmother the same way, even though her English vocabulary topped out at maybe two hundred words, even though I watched her face do something small and confused every time, a kind of recalibrating, before she'd either repeat herself in broken English or just let the thread drop. I told myself she understood more than she let on. I told myself this went on for almost a year, and it worked, in the sense that my accent flattened out and nobody at school commented on my house sounding foreign anymore.

What it also did was slowly wall my grandmother out of my daily life. Our conversations shrank to logistics - food, homework, whether I'd locked the door - because anything with nuance required a language I had decided I was too good, or too embarrassed, to keep using. She had stories about growing up during a typhoon that flooded her town for two weeks, about my grandfather courting her with letters he couldn't really write and had a neighbor draft for him. I know these stories now only in fragments, secondhand, because I spent a year making sure I wouldn't have to sit through them in the language they actually lived in.

I started speaking Tagalog again the following summer, clumsily, after I noticed how much my grandmother's face changed when I managed a full sentence, like a door had opened that she'd stopped expecting to open. It came back faster than I thought it would, muscle memory more than knowledge, but a year is a long time to withhold yourself from someone who has less time left than you do. I think about that gap more than almost anything else from those years, the version of myself who thought fitting in was worth that particular cost and didn't fully register what he was paying.

What I would bring to a campus is not some neat resolution to that story, because I don't think there is one. It's the specific attentiveness of someone who has watched a language nearly slip away and knows exactly how ordinary and how quiet that kind of loss can be - no dramatic scene, just a year of small refusals adding up. I notice, now, when someone's grandparent is sitting at the edge of a gathering not quite following the English around them, and I go sit next to them and ask what language they'd rather use. I bring the particular discomfort of having gotten something wrong that can't be fully undone, only kept from happening again, and the habit that discomfort built in me of not letting anyone go quiet at the edges of a room if I can help it.

It was cleared in the seventies for a reservoir project, and the people were relocated to a town nine kilometres away with better roads and a school and no history. He was fourteen. He has told me about it perhaps two hundred times, and until I was fifteen I heard almost none of it, because he tells stories in a loop and I had decided, somewhere around age eleven, that the loop meant nothing new was coming.

When I was sixteen I decided to fix this. I was going to record him. I had a plan and a phone and a list of questions, and I was going to build an oral history - that is genuinely the phrase I used, to myself, in my own head - a proper document of a place that no longer existed, so it would not be lost.

It did not work, and the way it did not work is what I want to write about.

The first session lasted forty minutes and I got almost nothing. I asked him what the village looked like. He described the temple. I asked how many houses. He said, many. I asked what his father did and he told me a story about a bullock that had already been told at three weddings. I pushed him with the questions I had prepared, the good ones, the ones about how it felt to leave, and he answered them in about eleven words each and then asked if I wanted tea.

I tried again a month later and it was worse, because by then he knew what I was doing and he performed. He gave me the version he gives to guests. He got dates wrong that I knew he knew. Halfway through he said, in Tamil, "you are writing a report," and it was not a compliment.

I gave up for nearly a year. I told myself he was old and it was too late, which was a comfortable thing to believe and also unfair to a man who does the crossword faster than I do.

What I did next was accidental. Last August, cooking, my mother needed a measure for rice and could not find the cup we use, and my grandfather went and got the brass one off the shelf and said, without anyone asking, that this was the padi his mother had used and that in Perumbakkam a bride's family sent one to the new house, and that theirs had been left behind in the move and this one was bought in the town afterwards to replace it, and that it was the wrong size, slightly, and his mother complained about it for eleven years.

That was more than I got in eighty minutes of interviews. He talked for an hour. I did not record it. I have thought about that a lot and I have decided I am not sorry.

So now I do not interview him. I cook with him. I ask about the thing in his hand. I have filled a notebook in fourteen months, badly, out of order, undated, and it contains more of Perumbakkam than my recordings ever would have.

The cup is still the wrong size. It holds about three-quarters of what it should.

I stopped playing the piano in March, after eleven years, and my mother has not forgiven me, and I am not sure she is wrong.

I want to put her case first, properly, because when people hear this story they arrive already on my side and that annoys me. Her case is not that she paid for it, though she did, for eleven years, forty minutes a week with Mrs Petrov and then with Mr Ainsworth after Mrs Petrov's hip. Her case is not even that I was good, though I was - Grade 8 at fifteen, distinction, the Wigmore Hall thing with the county youth orchestra where I did not play a wrong note in the Poulenc and have never once been able to enjoy the recording.

Her case is that quitting is a decision made by a version of me that will not be here in ten years, on behalf of a version of me who will be, and who will want it back and will not be able to have it.

She has evidence for this. She played the violin until she was nineteen and stopped when she went to university, and she has said, more than once, in a completely flat voice, that it is the thing she regrets. She has a violin in the loft. She has not opened the case since we moved.

So when she says you will regret this she is not guessing. She is reporting.

My case is harder to say without sounding ungrateful. It is not that I hate the piano. I do not hate the piano. It is that I had stopped being able to tell the difference between playing and being seen to play. Somewhere around Grade 7 the instrument became a thing I was measured by, and after that every hour at the keyboard had a small auditor sitting in it. I would learn a piece and my first thought at the end of it was never that was beautiful, it was that's about eighty per cent.

And it was consuming everything. Two hours a day, which is not a boast, it is an accounting. Two hours a day is fourteen a week, is the reason I have never had a Saturday job, is the reason I stopped drawing at thirteen.

The argument itself was not one argument. It was about eight, over four months, in kitchens and cars. She said: you are throwing away eleven years. I said: I am not throwing them away, I have them, they are in my hands. She said: they will go. And this is the sentence I have not been able to answer, because she is factually right. It does go. I am worse now than I was in March. I sat down at my grandmother's in August and my left hand had already got stupid.

What I said back was that I would rather lose something I had than keep spending my life defending it. She said that was the kind of thing you say at seventeen. Which - again - is a fair point that I cannot disprove for about a decade.

We do not really talk about it now. She has stopped mentioning it, which is worse than the arguing. The piano is still in the front room and nobody has suggested selling it and I do not know what that means. Sometimes I play in the evenings when the house is empty, badly, sight-reading things I have no business attempting, and I like it more than I liked any of the exams, and I have not told her that because she would take it as proof.

Maybe it is proof. Maybe in fifteen years I will have a violin in a loft of my own and I will understand exactly what she was trying to save me from, and I will not be able to explain it to my own child either.

But I am seventeen now, and it is my two hours a day, and the person who has to spend them is me. That is the whole of my argument, and I know it is not enough, and I did it anyway.

I worked Thursday and Friday nights, ten until six, from the week I turned sixteen. My mother's hours had been cut and we had a plan about it that we did not discuss much. The warehouse is a hundred and ninety thousand square feet of racking under lights that never change, and there is no window anywhere in the picking area, so time inside it is measured entirely by the gun. It tells you where to go. Aisle, bay, level, quantity. You go, you scan, you take, you scan again, and it gives you the next one. It also tells you how fast you are doing it. There is a number in the corner of the screen that is your rate against target, and it updates constantly, and I would like to say I ignored it but I did not ignore it once in eleven months.

What the gun taught me, more than anything, is what it feels like to be measured by something that cannot see you. On a bad night the number goes red and there is no argument to make. It does not know that bay 14 in aisle J has a light out and you have to read the labels by phone torch. It does not know that the tote you just filled with forty-eight litres of fabric softener is heavier than the one the person ahead of you got. It is not unfair, exactly. It is just indifferent, which I found was a different and stranger thing.

I got fast. By spring I was running about a hundred and ten percent of target most nights, and I understood by then that this was not a virtue, it was a set of small tricks: hold the gun in your left hand so your right is free, walk the aisle in the direction that makes the next pick shorter, learn which SKUs come in cases you can split with a thumb. A warehouse has one, and it is the number, and because the number is so obviously stupid, everyone quietly agrees to judge each other by something else instead.

He would write to me in English and I would answer in Portuguese, and then I would add a line at the bottom fixing his prepositions. I thought this was generous. I thought we were trading. I was, in my head, a very good friend who was helping. In April of that year he stopped replying for eleven weeks.

I had a whole theory about why. He had gotten bored of me, my Portuguese had gotten good enough that I was no longer interesting, he had real friends. I constructed all of that from nothing and I mostly stopped messaging, out of pride.

In July he came back and told me that his father had lost the shop in March and that they had moved to his aunt's in Contagem and that he had been working afternoons. It was in the first paragraph. He was not being dramatic about it. And then he said something that I have not gotten over, which was that he had wanted to tell me in March but that writing to me had started to feel like homework.

I had spent two years teaching myself his language and I had learned nothing about how to be talked to. Every correction I sent was a small signal that the point of the exchange was performance. I had made a friend into a practice partner and I had done it while congratulating myself.

What I did after that is the only part I am proud of. I stopped correcting anything, permanently. And I changed how I study, which sounds unrelated but isn't. When you have no teacher, the temptation is to become your own teacher - to grade everything, including other people. What I actually needed was to become my own student, which means being wrong out loud, at length, without a red pen anywhere in the room. My Portuguese got noticeably worse for about three months after I stopped optimizing and started just talking. Then it got much better, and it got better in a different direction: I can now argue in it, and be unclear in it, and say something badly and try again.

Léo and I have never met. We talk maybe twice a week. He is doing a technical course in electronics and he sends me photographs of circuit boards with captions I do not always understand. I got a weird look from the same librarian, Ms. Petrakis, roughly every Tuesday, because I always came in around four and always left with the next book in sequence, like I was working through a syllabus nobody had assigned me.

Here's the thing I got wrong, and I still think about it more than I'd like to admit. I told everyone - my parents, my friend Iris, a college counselor who asked about my summer during a mock interview in October - that the project was about discipline. About proving to myself I could finish something boring for the sake of finishing it. That was the story I told because it sounded like the kind of thing that belongs in an essay like this one.

It wasn't really true. Or it was true, but it wasn't the reason.

The actual reason, which I only admitted to myself much later, on a bus somewhere around November, staring out the window instead of doing precalc homework, was that I didn't want to choose. Choosing a book felt like a small failure waiting to happen - what if I picked wrong, what if I wasted a week on something forgettable when I could have read something that mattered. The shelf took the choosing away from me. It let me read forty-one books without ever being responsible for a single one of those decisions.

I've turned this over so many times since. Was that cowardice, dressed up as discipline? Some nights I think yes, obviously, and I feel a little embarrassed about the whole thing, about presenting a fear of choosing as some admirable feat of willpower. I finished the shelf. I can't fully tell you why. I've stopped needing to.

My grandmother and I have been arguing for four years about a notebook. My Cantonese was kitchen Cantonese, a few nouns and please and thank you. Her English was numbers, some curse words she'd picked up from my uncle, and the word "no," which she deployed with tremendous versatility. We should have had nothing to say to each other. Instead we had the stove.

She started teaching me by putting a knife in my hand and moving it herself, her fingers closed over mine, guiding the angle until I could feel in my wrist what she meant instead of hearing it. She never once told me a temperature or a time. She would touch the side of the wok, listen to the oil, watch the color of the scallions, and nod, and that nod was the whole recipe. When I asked how much ginger, she held up her hand and shrugged, which I eventually understood to mean: enough. Enough is not a measurement I could write down, but I tried anyway.

That's where the notebook started, and where the disagreement started with it. I wanted to fix what she was doing so it wouldn't disappear when she did. She wanted the opposite - she wanted it to live only in hands, mine included, the way it had lived in hers since her mother taught her in a village kitchen with no electricity. To her, writing it down was a kind of coffin. To me, not writing it down felt like standing next to something on fire and doing nothing.

We have never settled this. I still write in the notebook when she isn't looking, sneaking notes about ratios she'd deny existed. She still finds it sometimes and makes the sigh. Last spring I tried to explain, badly, in the mixed language we'd built between us, that I was scared of forgetting her exact way of doing things once she wasn't there to correct me. It wasn't over. It still isn't. For four years I sang in a church choir I did not believe in, and the thing I taught myself there was how to read music, which nobody ever sat down and explained to me.

I joined because my grandmother asked. She had sung in that choir since before my mother was born, and when her knees got bad she wanted somebody in the family holding the alto line. I said yes the way you say yes to a grandmother. I was thirteen and I had already quietly decided that I did not believe any of it, and I did not tell her that, and I still haven't.

Nobody in the choir taught anyone anything. That is not a complaint, it's just how it worked. The director handed out photocopied sheets on Thursday, played the alto line once on the piano, and then we sang. If you could not read the page you learned by ear, which most people did, and which I did for the first eight months. I would follow the woman beside me, half a beat behind, and hope.

The habit started because I was embarrassed. On the bus home from Thursday rehearsal, twenty minutes, I would put the sheet on my knees and try to work out which mark meant which sound. I had the melody in my head from rehearsal, so I had the answer key. All I had to do was match the shape on the paper to the shape in my memory. Up meant up. A filled-in note went past faster than a hollow one. Two lines and then a dot after a note meant it stretched.

Twenty minutes on a bus, once a week, for four years. That is the whole method. I never bought a book. I never looked anything up until much later, and when I finally did I found out I had gotten the names wrong for almost everything - I called the flat sign "the little b" for two years - but the system underneath was right, because I had built it out of things I could actually hear.

What learning it that way showed me is that I am much slower and much more stubborn than I thought I was. I did not have a breakthrough. There was no Thursday where it suddenly made sense. There was a Thursday about a year and a half in when the director put a new piece in front of us, something we had never heard, and I opened my mouth and the right note came out, and I remember being more suspicious than pleased. I thought it was luck. It happened again the next week.

I still sing there. I still don't believe it. My grandmother knows now - she asked me directly two winters ago and I did not lie to her, and she said that was fine and that I should keep coming, and I have. The disagreement is not settled and I do not think it will be.

But I can sight-read now, more or less, and I got it entirely off a bus seat with a photocopy on my knees, and I know exactly how long it took because I was there for every one of those twenty-minute pieces. It has made me distrust anyone who says a thing can be learned quickly. Mostly it has made me patient with the version of myself who is still bad at something, because that version is the one who does the actual work.

The chicken needed 200. I sang in the church choir for five years without believing a word of it, and for most of that time I thought this made me a hypocrite. The moment I stopped thinking so happened in a rehearsal in a cold building in February, and it changed more than my opinion of myself.

I stayed because I liked it. By fourteen I had stopped believing in God, quietly and without drama, the way you stop believing in a rumour when nobody produces evidence. I did not tell anyone. I kept turning up, and I kept singing about a resurrection I did not think had happened, and I felt like a fraud every single Sunday.

I had a private argument running in my head for about three years. It went: these words are claims. To sing a claim is to assert it. To assert something you think is false is to lie. Therefore I am lying, beautifully, in four-part harmony, for four pounds.

Then February. We were learning the Allegri Miserere, which is too hard for a parish choir, and we had been on the same eight bars for forty minutes. Sylvia, who directs, stopped us because the altos were flat on a suspension. She said something I have thought about ever since. She said: you are not holding that note for yourself, you are holding it so the sopranos have something to be dissonant against.

That is a technical instruction, about tuning. But I sat there with my folder open and understood, suddenly and physically, that I had been wrong about what I was doing.

A suspension only exists as a relationship. My note, alone, is neither right nor wrong. It becomes something when it rubs against the note above it and then resolves. Nobody in the building can hear my line as a line. What they hear is the whole chord, which is made of four people each holding something incomplete.

I had been treating singing as a series of statements I personally issued. It is not. It is a structure that four people build together, and the alto part is not a sentence I say, it is a piece I carry so that the thing can stand up. Whether I believe the words is a question about me. Whether the chord tunes is a question about us.

I am not claiming this solved theology. I still do not believe in God, and I do not think singing solves anything about that. What changed was my understanding of participation. I had assumed you could only legitimately take part in something you privately endorsed, that sincerity was the entry requirement for everything. But most of the things human beings do together are not like that. You hold a line so that someone else's line means something. That is not fraud. That is how a chord works, and, I have come to think, how quite a lot else works too.

After that I stopped apologising to myself on Sundays.

I sang my last service in December. Sylvia gave me a pencil, because I had never once brought one in five years. The new thing I understand about myself is that I do not need to agree with a room in order to be honestly of use to it, and I learned that from being flat on a suspension in a freezing church.

It wasn't me. It was never entirely me.

It is a Zenit-E, Russian, heavy as a brick, and its selenium light meter died sometime before I was born. The needle sits at the bottom of its little window and does not move, no matter how much light you throw at it.

My uncle's position is simple. He thinks I should have bought a cheap digital camera, or used my phone, and spent the four years I spent learning exposure on something that would actually get me somewhere. He is not unkind about it. He says it the way you'd tell someone their shoelace is untied.

What I taught myself was how to guess. There is a rule photographers used before meters, called Sunny 16: on a bright cloudless day, set your aperture to f/16 and your shutter speed to whatever your film speed is, and you'll be roughly right. Everything else works outward from there. Overcast, open up two stops. Shade under a building, three. Late gold light an hour before dark, another two. I found this on a forum, written by a man who signed his posts with the name of a town in Wales, and I did not believe him for about six months.

The way you stop not believing is you waste film. I wasted a great deal of it. A roll of thirty-six frames cost about two hundred rupees to buy and another two hundred to develop, and my first eleven rolls came back with maybe four usable pictures each. My mother thought I was throwing money into a hole. My uncle thought so too, and said so, and I remember the specific afternoon he stood in our kitchen holding a strip of my negatives up to the tube light and saying, gently, that a machine could do this in a hundredth of a second and never be wrong.

He is right about that. That is the part of the disagreement I cannot win and have stopped trying to.

What I would say back, if I could say it in a way that landed, is that being wrong slowly taught me something being right instantly would not have. By roll twenty I could walk out of a building and know, before I lifted the camera, that it was f/8 at a two-fiftieth. Not because I'd calculated it. Because my eyes had been corrected four hundred times. I learned that a skill without a teacher is mostly a long argument with your own confidence, and that the feedback loop matters more than the instruction - a week between shooting and seeing is a brutal way to learn anything, and it is also why the lessons stuck.

We still argue about it. He asked me last month what I plan to do with it, meaning the camera, meaning the four years. I said I didn't know. He nodded like that proved his point, and maybe it does.

I have a picture of him from that kitchen afternoon. The light through the window was doing something I'd never have caught with a meter telling me the average. I never showed it to him.

For two summers I was a lifeguard at a pool that almost nobody used. Tuesday and Thursday mornings, half six to half nine, at the leisure centre where the early session had maybe four regulars and some weeks had one. So what I mostly did was sit in a high chair above eight lanes of undisturbed water and watch nothing happen.

Nobody teaches you that part. The qualification teaches you rescues. You spend a weekend hauling a rubber dummy off the bottom and learning how to get someone out with a suspected spinal injury, and you come away thinking the job is the emergency. It isn't. The job is the four hundred hours before the emergency, and there is no course for that, and I had to work it out on my own, badly, over two years.

What I got wrong is simple to state and took me a long time to see.

I thought watching was a thing you did with your eyes. So I kept them open and I kept them pointed at the water, and I thought that was the job being done. And because almost nothing ever happened, I had no way of knowing whether I was doing it well. There is no feedback. If you watch perfectly for three hours, the result is that nothing happens. If you watch terribly for three hours, the result is also, almost always, that nothing happens. Those two mornings look identical from the outside and, more dangerously, they feel identical from the inside.

So I drifted. I want to be honest about how far. I was not on my phone - that would have got me sacked and I knew it. But I was in my own head. I planned things. I had long arguments with people who were not there. I would come out of a stretch and genuinely not be able to tell you whether the man in lane three had been swimming or resting for the last four minutes, and I would tell myself that if something had happened I would have noticed, because I was looking.

That is the thing I still think about: I was looking at the water for three hours and seeing it for perhaps forty minutes of that, and I had no idea, because looking and seeing use the same muscles from where I was sitting.

What broke it was small. A woman, one of the regulars, got out of the pool one morning and stood at the shallow end holding the rail for a while, and I clocked it and assumed she was catching her breath. She was there maybe ninety seconds. Then she left. And afterwards - an hour afterwards, in the changing room corridor - I found out from the receptionist that she had felt faint and gone and sat in reception for twenty minutes before driving home.

Nothing happened. That is the point. Nothing happened and I still had not seen it. She was six metres from me in my direct line of sight and I had processed her as scenery.

After that I stopped trusting my eyes and started building a system, which is the actual thing I taught myself. I gave myself a route: near lane, far lane, deep end, shallow end, the doors, back to the near lane, and I did it as an actual circuit, and I made myself name what I saw silently. Blue cap, breaststroke, steady. If I could not name it I had not seen it. I also learned that ten minutes standing up is worth thirty sitting down, and that if I let myself get warm I was finished, so I would take the cover off the chair.

Any experienced guard would tell you the scan pattern in a sentence. But there wasn't an experienced guard there at half six, and so I invented a worse version of something that already exists, which I have since decided is what most self-teaching actually is.

The larger thing it showed me is about attention rather than swimming pools. I had assumed attention was a state - that you were either paying it or not, and that a conscientious person paid it. It isn't a state. It's a task, and it decays, and it decays invisibly, and the only defence is a structure you impose on yourself from outside because you cannot feel it going.

I still think about the woman on the rail. She was fine. She came back the following Tuesday. But I sat in a high chair looking directly at her and did not see a person in trouble, and I would have sworn on anything that I was watching.

Okonkwo Trading and the customers say Auntie Mercy. I want to write about a thing I got wrong, which took me about four years to understand and which I still think about when I am supposed to be doing other work.

Here is the wrong thing. For most of my childhood I thought my mother's business was a stage she was passing through. Not because she said so. Because everything around me said so. School said so, in the way careers evenings never once mentioned resale or market trading. My friends said so, in the way they asked what my mum did and I said she works in retail and let them assume a shop with a till and a manager. I said it in that specific way, retail, because it was a word that sounded like it had a ceiling I could point to. And I said it to her, once, when I was fourteen and angry about something unrelated: that she should get a proper job.

I have replayed that sentence more times than I would like to admit. She did not shout. She said, in English, which she uses for arguments the way other people use a raised voice, that a proper job is one that pays for your shoes, and I was wearing shoes, and would I please pass the tape.

What I got wrong was not just rudeness. It was a whole model of what work is. I thought a proper job was one that somebody else had designed and you stepped into. I did not see that my mother had designed hers.

She has a system. She buys in bulk from a clearance broker in Erith, sacks sorted by category and grade, and she pays for grade three because grade one is a con - the margin is worse and the broker has already taken out the good pieces. Then she opens the sacks on the garage floor and does the sorting herself, and this is the part I did not understand for years. She is not sorting by size or by colour. She is sorting by customer. There is a pile for Mrs Adeyemi who wants long skirts with pockets. There is a pile for the girls who come after college and want anything that photographs well. There is a pile for church, which is separate from the pile for work, though a stranger could not tell the two apart. She holds a jacket up for four seconds and she is not looking at the jacket. She is running through about sixty people she knows.

That is not a market stall. That is a customer database held entirely in one woman's head, and it is more accurate than anything I could have built for her, and I know because I tried. When I was fifteen I made her a spreadsheet. I was very pleased with it. It had dropdowns. She used it for eleven days and then stopped, and when I asked why, she said it took longer to write down what she already knew than to know it. She was right and I was annoyed about her being right for most of a year.

I had absorbed, without noticing, the idea that second-hand is what you do when you cannot afford first-hand - that the business existed inside somebody else's failure. Women who could go to Next and don't, because a coat for eight pounds that will last four winters is not a compromise, it is arithmetic. Men buying suits for interviews. I got into sewing costumes for the Marlow Players the way most people get into anything at fifteen, which is that my mother volunteered me. Their wardrobe mistress had broken her wrist three weeks before a production of Blithe Spirit, and my mother, who had once heard me say I could use a sewing machine, offered my Saturdays without consulting me.

I could use a sewing machine in the sense that I had made a drawstring bag in Year 8.

For about eighteen months after that I thought of the whole thing as a chore I was too polite to get out of. I was good at it fairly quickly - I have decent hands and I can read a pattern - and I did not enjoy it. It was a church hall with a strip light that hummed, and a rail of donated clothing that smelled of other people's houses, and a group of adults between forty and seventy who had opinions about hemlines. I did what I was asked. I altered things. I turned a 1980s bridesmaid dress into something that could pass for 1927 if the audience was more than four rows back. I let out trousers for a man called Gordon three times in one season and did not ask why.

I told people I did it for the UCAS form. I think I believed that.

The thing that changed my mind happened during a production of A View from the Bridge, which is a play I did not know and had not read. I was making a work shirt for Eddie, the longshoreman, from a pattern I had drafted myself because we could not find anything that was right. The man playing him was called Ray, mid-fifties, a plumber, not a good actor in any technical sense - he had two volumes and a habit of looking at the floor on his own lines.

At the third fitting I had put the shirt on him and was pinning the shoulder, and I asked him to lift his arm so I could check the range, and he lifted it, and something happened to how he was standing. I do not know how to describe it better than that. He stopped being a plumber in a church hall wearing a shirt with pins in it. His weight went into his heels. His hands hung differently. He said, to nobody, "this is what he'd wear," and then he did about four lines of a scene we were nowhere near rehearsing, quietly, into the middle distance, and they were the first lines I had heard him say that sounded like a person.

He apologised afterwards. He said he'd got carried away.

I went home and thought about the shoulder seam. I had put it about two centimetres wider than his actual shoulder, deliberately, because a workman's shirt from 1955 is cut for movement and not for fit, and the effect of a wider shoulder seam is that the sleeve hangs from further out, and the arm swings from a different place, and you cannot hold yourself the way a man in a modern shirt holds himself. I had made a decision about a seam allowance and it had walked into the room ahead of him.

That was the turn. Before that I thought costume was decoration - the thing you put on top of the acting so the audience knows what year it is. After that I understood it as the opposite: a set of physical constraints and permissions applied to a body, which the body then has to answer. A corset does not make you look like a Victorian woman. It makes you breathe like one, and everything else follows from the breathing. A cassock does not signify a priest. It makes you take shorter steps.

I have done nine productions now. I have made a hooped skirt out of curtain wire and a great deal of swearing. I have learned to ask actors how they intend to move before I cut anything, which nobody taught me and which most amateur wardrobe departments do not do. I have started keeping a notebook of what I call solved problems: how to make a fat suit that does not slide, how to age a jacket with sandpaper and cold tea, how to build a quick change into a garment that also has to look like it has buttons.

I would like to study this properly, and I am aware that "I sew" sounds like a hobby. It is not a hobby. It is the study of how clothing writes instructions to a body, and I found it in a church hall under a humming light, and I did not notice what I had found for a year and a half because I was too busy resenting my mother for signing me up.

Gordon still needs his trousers let out. I still do not ask.
