I spent an entire year preparing for the mathematics olympiad.

Not just preparing - consumed by it. I'd wake up at five in the morning to work through problem sets. I'd stay after school to meet with the olympiad coach. I'd do problems until my eyes hurt and my hands cramped. I convinced myself that winning the olympiad was going to define my entire future, that it was the most important thing I could do in high school.

My parents were supportive, which meant they asked me every evening if I'd practiced, if I was making progress, if I thought I was going to win. My friends got used to me canceling plans because I had to study. I turned down social activities, skipped parties, missed events I actually wanted to go to because I was supposed to be training for this competition.

The week before the olympiad, I was confident. Not cocky, but genuinely confident. I'd solved so many problems that hard problems didn't feel as hard anymore. I understood the concepts deeply. I was ready.

I wasn't ready.

The actual olympiad was harder than anything I'd practiced. Not just slightly harder - completely different in a way I hadn't anticipated. The problems required approaches I hadn't developed. They tested edges of mathematics that I had gaps in. I left the competition feeling devastated, knowing I'd failed before the results even came out.

When the results were published, I was even further down the rankings than my worst fears had predicted. I was in the bottom half. My score was below average. All of that year of work, all of those early mornings and canceled plans and single-minded focus, and I'd still failed at the actual thing.

I think I spent about a week being genuinely depressed about it. I remember my mum trying to tell me that it didn't matter, that I'd learned so much through the process, that failing at the olympiad didn't mean I was bad at math. None of that landed. I'd failed at the thing I was supposed to succeed at. That's what mattered.

What messes me up still is that I don't think the failure was necessarily about my intelligence or my work ethic. I think I just didn't have the kind of creative problem-solving brain that makes you good at olympiad math. I could memorize techniques and solve problems I'd seen before. I couldn't generate novel approaches to problems I'd never seen. That's not a failure of effort. That's a limitation of my brain.

But also, I don't regret the year I spent training. I learned mathematics at a depth that I probably wouldn't have otherwise. I developed stamina for difficult problems. I learned how to sit with the feeling of not knowing something and work through it anyway. Those things are useful. They're real.

What I'm still wrestling with is how to think about effort when effort doesn't result in success. There's this narrative that if you just work hard enough, you'll achieve whatever you want. But I worked as hard as I could, and I still failed. So either the narrative is wrong, or I didn't work hard enough, or I'm not capable of succeeding at this thing. I'm not sure which one it is.

My friends don't really know how much I still think about this. They probably think it's weird that I'm sad about something from a year ago that I ultimately overcame. But I think about it because it taught me something that nobody wanted me to learn: that there are real limits to what hard work can achieve. That sometimes you try your absolute best and you still fail. That has to be okay if I'm going to actually be okay.

We moved from Bangkok to Stockholm when I was nine. My parents didn't ask me if I wanted to move. They didn't ask my younger sister or my older brother either. It was a job opportunity for my father. It was one of those adult decisions that children are simply expected to absorb without complaint. So we absorbed it.

The first winter was the thing that I don't think we were prepared for. Not prepared in the practical sense - we bought coats and boots and heating systems worked fine. We were unprepared in a different way. We didn't know what being cold all the time would do to us, to our family, to the way we related to each other.

My mother hated it. She said it from the first week and kept saying it every day after that. The darkness. The snow that was beautiful for the first month and then just kept existing, kept needing to be moved and walked through and dealt with. The way the city looked like it was shutting down at three in the afternoon because the sun went down. The way people seemed to disappear into their houses and there was no street life, no spontaneous gathering of neighbors, no flowing in and out of public spaces the way there had been in Bangkok.

My father loved it. He said the snow was beautiful and the winter air was crisp and the skiing was incredible and people were friendlier than he expected. He would come home excited about things he had done, places he had been, and my mother would listen with visible irritation. She didn't want to hear about how wonderful winter was. She was stuck inside because of winter. She was isolated because of winter. She was slowly being erased by winter, or at least that's how she talked about it.

What made it an argument is that they couldn't leave it alone. They didn't have one conversation about whether we would stay or go. They had fifty conversations. My mother would suggest moving back to Bangkok or maybe to somewhere warmer. My father would say we had committed to three years. My mother would say she couldn't do three years. My father would point out that the kids were adapting. My mother would argue that adapting to something terrible was not a virtue. On and on. Through that entire winter and into the spring.

My brother tried to stay out of it. My sister cried sometimes but didn't really understand what the argument was actually about. I understood that my mother was lonely and my father was happy, and that these two things were directly opposed to each other. If he stayed happy about Stockholm, she had to stay sad about it. If she convinced him to leave, they could both be home. But he wasn't convinced.

What's unresolved is that my mother's sadness and my father's joy both turned out to be true. She really was isolated. Winter really was hard for her. And he really did love it. Really did find something there that he wasn't finding elsewhere. Neither of them was wrong. They just had irreconcilable experiences of the same place.

We ended up staying the three years. Then we ended up staying longer. Now we've been here for seven years. My mother learned Swedish. She found community. She's not happy exactly, but she's built a life. My father got promoted. He has friends. He takes every opportunity to ski.

But that argument never fully resolved. It just stopped being active. It's still there underneath, the feeling that my mother sacrificed something to make my father happy. That my father was insensitive to her suffering. That they made different choices about this place and they're both correct about it.

I think about it now because I'm applying to universities and some of them are far from home. I keep thinking about my mother's winter, about being somewhere that doesn't fit you, about the cost of loving someone who loves something you hate. I don't know if I'm afraid of becoming my mother or afraid of becoming my father. But that first winter taught me something about the difference between compromise and resentment. Between staying somewhere and staying somewhere while being angry about it. My parents stayed together through that winter, but they never quite agreed about it. That's a kind of way to live, I guess. I just know it's harder than it looks.

We moved from Cebu to Winnipeg in August, which everyone told us was the easy month, and by November I understood what they meant by easy, because by December the easy part was long gone and the temperature stopped making sense to me as a number and started just meaning pain in a specific spot on my face.

My father's solution to almost everything that first winter was the same: put on your boots, we're walking to the corner store. It didn't matter if we needed anything. Some nights we walked the six blocks there and back and came home with a single carton of milk we didn't need, because the walk itself was the point, though he never explained it that directly. He said only that if we hid inside all winter waiting for it to feel normal, it would never feel normal, and that the fastest way through was through, on foot, every single evening, in whatever the temperature happened to be.

I hated it for the first month. My eyelashes froze on the walk home more than once. I complained the whole six blocks some nights, in Tagalog, so the few people we passed wouldn't understand exactly how much I was suffering. Somewhere around January the walk stopped being a punishment and started being the one part of the day I could count on. We started recognizing the same people at the corner store, the same dog walker, the same old man who cleared his own walk and half of his neighbor's without being asked. My father would nod at him every night, and eventually they started talking, mostly about the snow, weeks before either of us kids knew the man's name. That's how we met Mr. Halvorsen, who later showed my father how to actually use a snowblower instead of shoveling by hand, which was the single most useful piece of information anyone gave us that entire winter.

I believed India was my home in the way people believe facts. It was the place I had always been, where my family lived, where school was a comfortable routine I had learned to navigate without thinking. I didn't think of myself as someone with a home - home was just the air around me, invisible and constant. The news came in May, right in the middle of tenth grade. We would leave in July. I told my friends and their responses ranged from jealousy to sympathy, but nobody really understood what I felt, which was a kind of panic I couldn't name. Singapore was a real place on a map, a place I could find in my geography textbook, but it was also a theoretical place, not a place where I had memories.

I spent the first month there in a fog. The school was clean and organized in a way that made everything feel sterile. The students were nice in a polite way that felt distant. My accent, which I had never noticed before because everyone around me had always sounded the same, suddenly announced itself constantly. Teachers would ask me to repeat things. Classmates' heads would turn when I spoke. For the first time I could remember, I sounded like someone who didn't belong.

But something happened around month three. I was walking home from school - we lived close enough to walk, which surprised me because I expected Singapore to be different, but it was just a place where people walked and lived and complained about homework like anywhere else. A girl from my English class caught up with me and asked if I wanted to get food. Her name was Iris and she was from Hong Kong and had moved there last year. We went to a place that made noodles, and she told me that the weird thing about moving was that you don't get to choose when you stop feeling like a visitor.

"You just wake up one day and you're not," she said, eating her noodles carefully to avoid dripping them on her uniform. "It's not a moment exactly. It's just the first day you don't think about how much you miss home."

I thought that was the most depressing thing I had ever heard, and I said so. Iris laughed and told me I was thinking about it wrong. "You don't stop missing it," she said. "You just learn that your brain isn't big enough to hold two places with the same amount of reality. So one of them gets smaller. That doesn't mean it's not real. It just means you're not living in it anymore."

That was in October. By the time winter break came around, I noticed something strange. When I video-called my friends in Delhi, I could barely imagine the places they were calling from. The streets I had walked a thousand times looked flat and distant on my screen. I wasn't sure if that made me a traitor to my own past or just a person living forward into my own life.

I still miss Delhi. But I stopped believing it was the only place I could belong. Home turned out to be more portable than I thought.

It started because of a chain, and it stayed going because of a chain, and if I am honest about the whole thing, most of what I have learned in the last four years I learned from chains.

The first one belonged to a boy named Theo, who was seven, and who lived four doors down from us on Whitcombe Road. He had come off his bike at the bottom of the hill and the chain had jumped the front ring and jammed itself between the ring and the frame, which is a thing that looks catastrophic to a seven-year-old and takes about ninety seconds to fix. I was thirteen. I was outside with a football and nothing to do. I knew how to fix it only because my own bike had done the same thing a month earlier and my dad had shown me once, impatiently, on his way to somewhere.

So I fixed it, and Theo went away, and that would have been the end of it except that a week later his sister knocked on our door with a bike that had a flat, and asked if I did that.

I did not do that. But I said yes.

That is the entire origin. There was no decision. There was a girl at the door and a word that seemed easier to say than no.

What followed was four years of a Saturday morning habit so small that I did not notice it becoming anything. Between about nine and eleven I would be out the front with whatever had turned up during the week. Punctures, mostly - there is a stretch of the cycle path near the industrial units that has been shedding glass since before I was born, and I have probably patched two hundred inner tubes that all failed within a hundred metres of the same spot. Brake pads worn to the metal. Gear cables stretched so far that only three of the seven gears worked, which children accept as normal, the way they accept everything. Saddles at the wrong height, which is the most common problem and the one nobody ever asks about, because a child does not know that a bike is supposed to be comfortable. They think the discomfort is them.

I learned by looking things up the night before and by getting things wrong. I put a tyre back on with the tube pinched under the bead and it blew out in the road twenty minutes later. I overtightened a bolt on a cheap aluminium crank and stripped the thread and had to tell an eight-year-old that his bike would not be ready that day, and watch him try to be fine about it. I bought a cone spanner set with birthday money because I had spent three weeks failing to service a wheel bearing with a pair of pliers and a lot of confidence.

The tools accumulated. There is a plastic crate now, in the shed, that is worth more than any bike I have ever worked on.

Here is what I did not expect, and what makes me want to write about this rather than about anything else I have done.

I know that street better than I know anything. Not the buildings - the households. I know that the Kowalczyks have three children and one bike between them and that the middle one is fastest and therefore gets it most. I know that Amara's father works nights and that she is quiet on Saturdays if he is sleeping. I know which families will offer me money and which will offer me food and which will do neither because they cannot, and I know that I must take the food and refuse the money in a way that does not embarrass anyone, and that this is a skill, and that nobody teaches it, and that I got it wrong for about the first year.

A bike is a strange object to be trusted with. It is the only thing most of those children own that is worth anything, and it is also the machine that decides how big their world is - whether they can get to the park, whether they can get to their cousin's, whether they are allowed to go to the shop alone. When Theo's chain jammed, his radius was about four hundred metres. When I unjammed it, it was three kilometres. Nobody says that out loud. But the parents know. It is why a woman I had never spoken to knocked on our door in 2022 with a bike and an apology and no expectation whatsoever, and why I stayed out until two that afternoon.

The habit is still going. It is smaller now - most Saturdays there is nothing, and I do coursework instead, and I have started to think about the fact that I am leaving. Theo is eleven and has been helping me since he was nine. He can do a puncture faster than I can. He cannot do a bottom bracket and does not want to learn, and I have decided not to push him, because the point was never the bottom bracket.

I want to study mechanical engineering, and I could give the neat version of why: that I love systems, that I like the honesty of a machine, that a bicycle is the most efficient thing a human being has ever built. All of that is true. But the real reason is quieter. It is that I have spent four years learning that a small competence, held steadily, in one place, over a long time, turns into something that is not really about the competence at all. I fixed chains. What I built was a street where a child knows there is someone to ask.

My uncle taught me to drive in a 1994 Ford F-150 with a manual transmission and a passenger door that only opened from the outside. We did it in the hay field behind his house in Cass County, where there was nothing to hit except one walnut tree and, in theory, the irrigation pump. He gave me exactly one rule that first afternoon: if you don't know what's about to happen, put in the clutch. Everything else, he said, we would figure out.

I was fourteen. I got good fast, or I thought I did. Within three weeks I could start on the hill by the culvert without rolling back, and I could downshift into second without the truck bucking, and I had started to enjoy the specific arrogance of a kid who can do something adults find difficult. By July I was driving the truck alongside the baler while my cousin Wes stacked bales in the bed, which meant holding a steady four miles an hour across uneven ground with a person standing up behind me.

The thing I got wrong happened on a Tuesday. Wes yelled something I could not hear over the tractor. I turned around to look at him. I did not put in the clutch, and I did not stop, and while I was turned around the truck drifted maybe six feet to the left, and the right rear tire dropped into a shallow washout. The truck lurched. Wes went down onto the bales and then off the side of the bed and landed on his back in the stubble.

He was fine. That is the part I have to say early, because it changes what kind of story this is. He got up, swore at me with real creativity, and had a bruise across his shoulder blades for two weeks. Nothing was broken. My uncle came over, looked at the washout, looked at me, and said, "You looked away," and then he had me get back in and finish the row, which at the time felt like cruelty and which I now understand was the whole lesson.

What I still think about is not the drift. Trucks drift. What I think about is why I turned around. Wes was yelling and I wanted to know what he was saying, and underneath that, I wanted him to see that I was the kind of driver who could hold a conversation while working. I had gotten good enough at the mechanics that I had started spending my attention on how I appeared instead of on what I was doing. The competence made me careless in a way that pure incompetence never had. When I was terrible at it, I stared at the field like it might attack me.

I have found that pattern in myself since, and I do not think I have solved it. It showed up in chemistry when I stopped writing out the intermediate steps because I could do them in my head, and then could not find my own error on the semester exam. It showed up in debate when I started improvising rebuttals because improvising looked better than reading from a flow sheet, and lost a round I should have won on the extended argument I forgot to extend. Both times the tell was the same: I was performing the task instead of doing it.

I do not have a clean method for catching it. What I have is Wes on his back in the stubble, and my uncle's flat sentence, and a physical memory of my own hands on a wheel I was not looking through. When I notice I am enjoying being observed, I try to put in the clutch. Sometimes I remember in time.

But it happened to ours.

The hospital was loud and fluorescent and everyone there seemed to know what they were doing except us. They ran tests and did scans and used words like "ischemic" and "prognosis" that didn't mean anything to me. What mattered was that he was alive and his brain was damaged and nobody could really tell us what that meant for his future. The doctors talked about recovery. The physical therapists talked about neuroplasticity. Everyone talked about the "window" where recovery was most possible, and that window was weeks, maybe months, and after that it got harder.

We came home with discharge papers and a list of exercises he needed to do. Daily. Repeatedly. The exercises were simple. Arm movements. Leg movements. Balance work. The theory was that by repeating them, his brain would rewire. New neural pathways would form. His body would relearn things it had forgotten.

My mom hired a physical therapist to come twice a week. But the rest of the time, between those visits, he needed to do the work. And my mom couldn't do it alone - she had to work to keep insurance. So I started helping. I'd come home from school and we'd go through the exercises. Twenty reps of this. Hold this for thirty seconds. Do that five times.

I watched YouTube videos about stroke recovery to understand what we were doing. I learned about motor cortex and muscle memory and why repetition mattered. I learned that every single repetition was theoretically helping his brain reorganize itself. I learned that motivation mattered because people gave up too easily. I learned all of this from various physical therapists and recovery specialists on YouTube, people I'd never met explaining their expertise to a camera.

What I didn't learn from YouTube is how to watch your father try to lift his arm and not quite get there. How to see him frustrated that his body wasn't doing what he wanted. How to hear him say things like "I used to be strong" with his voice breaking. YouTube doesn't teach you how to keep showing up every single day to do something that feels like it's not working. By month four something shifted. He could lift his arm higher than he could before. He could walk further. The progress was real and measurable. The mosquitoes at Hobart Marsh are a specific problem that nobody warns you about properly. People say "bring bug spray." What they mean is that between roughly 6:40 and 8:15 in the morning, in late July, you will be inside a cloud, and the cloud will have opinions.

I spent two summers there. The first one was because my aunt knew someone at the county conservation district and I needed a job. The second one was because I wanted to go back.

The work is not interesting to describe. You walk transects. A transect is a straight line you have decided on in advance, and you walk it, and at fixed intervals you stop and put down a quadrat, which is a square made of PVC pipe, and you write down every plant species inside the square. Then you move. Then you do it again. My supervisor, a woman named Bett who has done this for nineteen years, can identify sedges from about four meters away, which I initially assumed was showing off and which I now understand is just what happens to a person after nineteen years.

I was bad at it for a long time. Sedges have edges, rushes are round - that is the rhyme, and it is true, and it is also almost useless in the field when the plant is half-submerged and has been chewed on. I misidentified Carex stricta as Carex lacustris so many times that Bett started making a noise when I said it.

The thing that changed was the data.

At the end of the first summer, I asked what happens to the sheets. Bett said they go into a database that goes back to 2004. I asked if I could see it. She said sure, in a tone that suggested nobody had asked before.

There were twenty years of quadrats. Same transects, same intervals, walked by a rotating cast of bored teenagers and one very patient adult. And when you plot it - I did this on my laptop over two weekends in September, badly, in a spreadsheet - you can see the cattails moving. Typha angustifolia. It comes in from the north edge where the culvert drains the road runoff, and between 2004 and now it has taken about sixty meters of the marsh, and it does not go backward.

Nobody had plotted it. The data existed. Everyone knew, in a general way, that there were more cattails. But the actual number - sixty meters, roughly three a year, accelerating after the 2011 road resurfacing - was sitting in a filing cabinet in a form nobody had looked at.

I showed Bett. She was quiet for a while and then she said "that's the salt," and then she explained about road salt and specific conductance and how cattails tolerate it and the sedges do not.

The second summer I still walked transects. But I also built a proper database, and I wrote a small script that flags any quadrat where the dominant species has changed from the previous year, and I made a map. The county used the map in a grant application. I do not know whether they got the grant.

What I took from this is not "I love wetlands," although I do. It is something narrower and more useful. Institutions collect enormous amounts of data and then do not look at it. This is not because anyone is lazy. It is because collecting is a job somebody is assigned and looking is a job nobody is assigned.

I want to study environmental science, with statistics. I am aware that this is an unglamorous combination. But somewhere there is a filing cabinet with twenty years of something in it, and I would like to be the person who opens it.

By the time I was thirteen I could keep a full scorebook faster than the official scorer the league sent, and my father, who captained the team and took the game more seriously than a grown man with a day job probably should, trusted my book over anyone's.

The semifinal was the exception. He was given out, caught behind, off a ball that everyone on our side of the boundary saw brush nothing but his pad. I saw it too. I was twelve feet away with the clearest angle in the ground. The umpire raised his finger anyway, and my father walked off without a word, which was its own kind of protest, because normally he'd have said something.

After the match he came and found me at the scorer's table and asked to see the book. He wanted me to change the dismissal. Not the runs, not the result - just the note beside his name, from "c Behind b Rathi" to something softer, "given," with a question mark, so that when people read the book years later they'd know it was disputed. He said the book was the only record that would outlast anyone's memory of the day, and he didn't want his name attached to an outcome he didn't believe in.

I told him no. I remember exactly how it felt to say it, my stomach folding in on itself, because I had never told my father no about anything that wasn't chores. I said the book records what the umpire decided, not what actually happened, that's the whole point of it, that's what makes it a real record instead of a story we tell ourselves. If I start changing entries because a player disagrees, the book stops meaning anything.

He didn't yell. He's not a yeller. He just looked at me for a second too long, said "fair enough," and walked to the car. We didn't talk about it again that day, or really ever, not directly. But he never asked me to change another entry, not once in the five more years I kept his books, even when I know he wanted to.

She used the word threshold and explained that every time I pushed past the point where he had already begun to panic, I was not teaching him that I come back. I was teaching him that panic is the ordinary condition of an afternoon. Eight months of careful, well-documented work had made him measurably worse, and my notebook was the record of it. I remember being irritated by this, which is an ugly thing to admit. She didn't talk much, mostly kept to her own row, and I filed her, without really examining why, as someone I didn't need to make an effort with, someone separate from the version of the summer I was having with the other teenagers on the crew who joked around and complained about the heat together at lunch.

About four weeks in, rushing to hit the count that got you a end-of-week bonus, I knocked a full flat of peaches off the back of the trailer. I stood there doing the math on how much that flat was worth against my hourly rate and understanding, with total clarity, that I was about to lose the bonus and possibly get written up on top of it.

Ofelia was two trees down. She didn't say anything to me. She walked over, looked at the flat for about two seconds, and started pulling perfect peaches out of her own bins to replace mine, fast, without a word, finishing before the foreman reached us and simply nodding at him when he glanced at my flat and moved on. It took me a second to understand what had actually happened, that she'd given up part of her own count, her own bonus, for a girl who up to that point had barely bothered to learn how to pronounce her name correctly.

I tried to thank her properly that afternoon and she waved it off, said something in Spanish to another picker that made them both laugh, and went back to her row like it hadn't cost her anything, though I knew by then exactly what a flat of peaches was worth to someone getting paid by the pound. I started paying attention to her after that in a way I hadn't bothered to before. I learned she had three grandchildren she was saving for, that she'd been the fastest picker on that crew for over a decade, that the thing I'd read as coldness in her was really just a woman who didn't waste words on people who hadn't earned them yet, and that I apparently hadn't, not for a month.

Here's the part I still think about. I never actually apologized for those first few weeks, for deciding she wasn't worth talking to before she'd done anything to me at all. I meant to, near the end of the summer, and kept not finding the right moment, and then the season ended the way seasons end, everyone scattering back to whatever the rest of their year looked like, and I never got her last name or a way to reach her. I went back the following June hoping to find her on the crew and was told she'd retired that spring after almost twenty years, and that was it, that was the whole ending, no goodbye, no thank-you that actually landed.

There is no double entry for that.

I still keep the accounts. He still does not look at them, and I have stopped offering. Twice a year, when the insurance renews, he asks me what I think, and I tell him, and we both act as though it is a normal question between two adults, which is its own kind of agreement.

That's the thing I got wrong and I still think about it.

"Apparently not."

"No. You know this. You did not check it."

What I had not done, not once in eleven weeks, was work a problem and then go back and verify the answer against the original conditions. I had been solving forward and never backward. The mechanics of it were always the same. We would sit in a room with pale walls and a poster about hand washing. The doctor would talk to me instead of to my mother, which I noticed early and did not have a word for. I would turn what he said into Gujarati, and I would turn her answer into English, and I would leave out the parts I judged unnecessary, and nobody ever checked my work.

That last part is the thing I want to write about, because I did not think about it at all for about six years.

I edited constantly. If my mother described a symptom in a way that sounded, to my nine-year-old ear or my thirteen-year-old ear, embarrassing or rambling, I compressed it. If she said something that I thought would make the doctor think less of her - if she mentioned a home remedy, or that she had waited four months before coming - I softened it or dropped it. I told myself I was being efficient. I was being protective, which felt like the same thing.

I changed my mind about all of it in a room at Sarvodaya Hospital when I was fifteen, in a consultation about my mother's hand.

She had had numbness in two fingers for a while. The doctor asked how long. She said, in Gujarati, a long sentence about how it had started around the time of Diwali when she was doing the cleaning, and how it was worse when she woke up, and how she had thought it was from the cold water, and how her sister in Rajkot had the same thing and it went away.

I said: about four months, worse in the mornings.

Which is a fine translation. It is arguably a better answer than the one she gave. It contains the medically relevant facts, and I was quietly pleased with myself for it.

The doctor nodded and wrote and asked something else, and my mother said something to me, quietly, not for translation - she said, tell him about my sister.

And I said, in English, that her sister had it too.

He put down the pen. He asked how old her sister was, and whether it had been diagnosed, and about six more questions I would never have thought to consider relevant, and the appointment went somewhere completely different from where it had been going.

I sat in that chair and understood that I had been doing this for six years. I had been standing in the middle of every medical conversation my parents had ever had in this country, editing, with no training and no oversight and total confidence.

I do not know what I lost them. That is the part I think about. There is no way to audit it. There were probably appointments where nothing was missed and there was possibly one where something was.

If it takes longer, it takes longer. I have said, out loud, to a doctor who was looking at his screen, that my mother is not finished.

Then he showed me the state framework, a spiral-bound thing listing eleven required topics for the semester, of which Homestead was not one. Then he showed me his own binder, tabbed, full of primary sources he had photocopied over twenty-two years, including a page of the Pinkerton testimony.

But it was the eleventh of June and his birthday was the nineteenth, and drying properly would have meant a month indoors, and I told myself that these were pallets, not furniture timber, and that it probably did not apply.

The bench was beautiful for about five weeks. My mother thinks that what I did last year was kind. We have been going round this for eight months and neither of us has moved.

I was a scribe. There is a boy in the year below me, Tomas, who is blind, and for two terms I sat in exams and in some lessons and wrote down what he said. Nobody trained me. There was supposed to be a training session and it was cancelled twice and then term started. So what I know about scribing I taught myself, in the room, while doing it, which is not a good way to learn anything and is how most people learn most things.

The first thing I learned was that I did not know what a scribe was for. I had assumed I was a pen. He would say words and the words would appear on the page and my job was to be transparent. That lasted about forty minutes. Because he would say a sentence and then stop and say "no, wait," and I would have written half of it, and now there was a decision to make about what to cross out that he could not see me making. Or he would spell a word and the spelling would be wrong and I would have to decide, in a fraction of a second, whether correcting it was help or cheating. There is no manual for that. Or if there is, it was in the training session that got cancelled.

I built my own rules. That is the honest version of "taught myself." I decided that I would read back everything, always, even when it was slow, even when he was impatient, because the alternative was that my version of his answer would go in and he would never know. I decided I would not fix spelling unless he asked, and that I would ask once at the start of every session whether he wanted me to. I decided that when he paused I would say "you're at, and therefore the pressure" and let him hear where he was, rather than waiting silently, because silence made him rush.

None of those rules were obvious. I got them wrong first. In the November mock I "helped" - he was going nowhere on a question and I read the question back with a slightly different emphasis, and the emphasis was a hint, and he took it. He got a better mark than he had earned. I have never told anyone that except my mother, and here.

Which is where the disagreement is.

My mother says I am being hard on myself. She says the whole point of an access arrangement is that the boy should not be disadvantaged, that a sighted student would have reread the question with their own emphasis anyway, that I am inventing a crime. She says this in the voice she uses when she has decided the conversation is finished. And she says the larger thing, which is that it was generous of me to do it at all, that most seventeen-year-olds would not have given up their frees, and that I should let myself have that.

I do not think it was generous. I think that is the part she will not hear. It was interesting. I wanted to be in the room. There is something in the mechanics of it - the exact latency between his sentence and my hand, the fact that a comma is a decision somebody has to make and normally the writer makes it and here it was me - that I found more absorbing than any lesson I sat in that year. That is not kindness. That is curiosity wearing a volunteer's badge, and being praised for it makes me feel like a fraud in a way I cannot explain to her without it sounding like fishing.

And the emphasis thing was real. She calls it a nothing. It was not a nothing to me because I felt the moment I did it - I felt myself decide to be liked rather than be accurate, which is exactly the failure mode a scribe has to not have.

We are not going to resolve it. I have stopped raising it. She thinks I have come round. What I have actually concluded is narrower: that the only reliable thing I learned without a teacher was where my own hand wants to go when nobody is checking, and that knowing that is not the same as being able to stop it. The habit was that I wrote down what people said, exactly, in a small notebook, and it got me into more trouble than anything else I have done.

I started doing it in ninth grade for a boring reason. I joined the school paper and my first assignment was a piece about the new cafeteria contractor, and I interviewed the vice principal and then went home and wrote up what he had told me, and when it was published he said he had not said that. I did not have proof. He was probably not lying either - I think he genuinely remembered it differently - but the piece got pulled and I got a talking-to and my byline was replaced with the word Staff.

So I bought a notebook. The kind with the elastic band. And from then on, whenever anybody said anything to me for a story, I wrote it as they said it, in the moment, with the date at the top of the page. Not summary. The words.

For two years this was invisible. It looked like a tic. People teased me for it - my friend Ravi used to say things very slowly in a fake official voice so I could keep up. I filled four notebooks. Most of what is in them is nothing: what time the bus leaves for the debate meet, somebody's guess about the exam schedule, three pages about a broken water cooler.

Then in eleventh grade I wrote a piece about the school's counselling office. It was not an exposé. It was supposed to be a service piece about how to book an appointment. But in reporting it I found out that eleven students had been told there was a waiting list, and that there was no waiting list, and that the actual situation was that the counsellor's hours had been reduced to one afternoon a week in September without anyone announcing it. I put that in the piece, four sentences, near the end.

The article ran on a Thursday. On Friday I was in the principal's office with my faculty advisor and a man from the district whose role was never explained to me, and I was told that I had misrepresented the school, and that the counsellor had never said her hours were cut, and that I had invented the number eleven.

I had page seventy-three of notebook three. Date, time, her office, her words, including the sentence about the reduction and including her saying that she had asked twice about it. And I had the eleven students, each with a page.

It did not go the way it does in a film. Nobody apologised. What happened was that the room got quiet and the man from the district asked to see the notebook and I said he could look at the page and not the notebook, which I am still a little proud of, and after about ten minutes they told me I could go and that the matter was closed. The article stayed up. In January the counsellor's hours went back to three afternoons and no announcement was made about that either.

I got a reputation out of it that I am not sure I wanted. Teachers are careful around me now. One of them said, half joking, that talking to me is like being deposed.

But I have kept doing it, and I have thought a lot about why the habit worked, and I do not think it is because it protected me. It is that writing down exactly what someone says forces you to hear exactly what they said, which is different from what you expected them to say, and the gap between those two is where every real story I have ever found has been sitting.

I am on notebook seven. Most of it is still nothing.

By the end of the two-week collection period, we had a hundred and thirty-seven kilos. People brought things in, sure. A family brought rice. Someone's mother sent dal. We got some canned vegetables. But the gap between what we'd promised and what we'd actually collected was so enormous it felt obscene.

The night we counted everything, I sat in the school gymnasium looking at the piles of food and felt absolutely sick. I'd been wrong about what was possible. I'd overestimated how much people cared, or how much they were willing to act on that care. I'd been wrong in the way that matters most - I'd made promises on behalf of a community that turned out not to be ready to make those promises.

Anaya wanted to just give out what we had and consider it done. I understood that impulse. It was the easy way out. But I couldn't stop thinking about the people we'd told would receive this food. I couldn't stop thinking about us going to them and saying, "We collected five hundred kilos," when we only had a little over a quarter of that.

So I told my parents about it.

This is where things got complicated, because my father disagreed with how I wanted to handle it. He said we should just give out what we'd collected, that trying to do more would exhaust us, that the families would be grateful for what they got and we shouldn't be so hard on ourselves. We'd tried, he said. We'd put in effort. That mattered. He wasn't wrong, exactly. But he was also saying we should keep the lie intact - the lie of the five hundred kilos, the lie that we'd managed to do what we'd promised.

I wanted to tell people the truth. I wanted to say that we'd failed at our goal, but here's what we'd actually managed, and here's what the actual need looks like, and here's what would actually help if people wanted to participate. I thought that truth, even though it was a failure, was more honest and more useful than pretending everything had gone according to plan.

We didn't resolve this. We still don't, really. My father was right that the families who received the food were grateful, that a hundred and thirty-seven kilos was better than zero. He was right that we put in genuine effort and that the effort was valuable. But I'm convinced he was wrong that we should have just accepted the gap between what we promised and what we delivered, and moved on.

I think about what we could have done differently. We could have set a more realistic goal. We could have been more transparent in our communications about what we were actually collecting. I still think I was right to push for honesty, even though it created conflict with my father. My grandmother taught me to cook without ever explaining anything, because she could not, and because I do not think she would have anyway. She came from Fuzhou at sixty-one and her English stayed at about thirty words, most of them nouns. My Mandarin is worse than her English and my Fuzhounese does not exist. So the arrangement we arrived at was this: on Saturday mornings I stood on her left side at the counter, and I did whatever she did, roughly a beat behind.

She would take a piece of ginger and hit it with the flat of the cleaver, and I would take a piece of ginger and hit it with the flat of the cleaver. If I did it wrong she took the cleaver out of my hand and did it again slowly, twice, and gave it back. If I did it right she said nothing whatsoever. She would dip a chopstick, touch it to her tongue, adjust, and dip again a minute later, and I had been standing next to this for a hundred and fifty Saturdays without registering it as a technique. I had been waiting for a recipe. She was not using one.

Our robot was named Gerald, which was voted on, which was a mistake.

The competition was FIRST Tech Challenge, the 2024 season, and the task involved picking up plastic hexagons and placing them on a scoring rack. That is a sentence that makes it sound simple. It is not simple. A hexagon is a shape with no good grip surface and six equally plausible orientations, and a scoring rack in a gymnasium is at a height that changes depending on how level the gym floor is, which is never.

Gerald had a two-stage linear slide, a differential drivetrain, and a gripper that we redesigned four times.

Version one used two opposing servos and a rubber pad. It worked perfectly on the workbench and failed immediately at the first scrimmage in Dayton, because on the workbench the hexagon was always presented to us in the same orientation by a human being, namely me. On the field the hexagons are wherever they land.

Version two added a passive compliant wrist, which is a phrase I learned from a paper that a mentor named Sanjay sent us and that I did not fully understand for about three weeks. The idea is that instead of making the gripper strong enough to force the object into alignment, you make the joint loose enough that the object aligns itself as you close. It is counterintuitive. You are making the machine weaker on purpose.

It cut our cycle time by roughly forty percent and it cost eleven dollars in printed parts.

Version three was worse than version two. We built it anyway because our team captain, Reyna, had designed it and everyone including Reyna had gotten attached to it before we tested it. It took us two weeks to admit this. We lost a scrimmage. The specific failure was that the new gripper's wider jaw fouled on the rack uprights at exactly the height we scored most often, which is a thing we would have found in twenty minutes if we had tested it on a real rack instead of a cardboard mock-up.

Version four was version two with a slightly longer wrist.

I have thought about that sequence a lot. We spent eleven days building something worse because it was ours, and we spent two more days not saying so. Nobody was being stupid. Reyna is the best engineer on the team and she was the first one to eventually say it out loud. The failure was structural: we had no rule that forced a design to be tested against the previous version before we committed to it.

So we made one. It is written on the whiteboard in the shop and it says: NEW BEATS OLD ON THE REAL FIELD, OR OLD STAYS. It is not elegant. It has saved us at least three bad decisions since.

We went 6-4 at the regional and did not advance. Gerald is currently disassembled in four bins in my garage, except for the wrist, which is on my desk.

I want to study mechanical engineering. Everyone on my team wants to study mechanical engineering, and I imagine every FTC kid who writes one of these essays says the same thing, so I will try to say something narrower.

What I actually learned is that most engineering failures I have seen were not technical. Version three was not defeated by physics. It was defeated by eleven days of nobody wanting to tell Reyna, and by the absence of a rule that would have made telling her unnecessary. The compliant wrist was a genuinely clever piece of mechanical design and it took three weeks to understand. The whiteboard rule took ten seconds to write and it was harder.

Gerald was a bad name. We should have tested that too.

What I was doing was collecting. I had a list. I ticked things off. When I saw a bird, the question I asked was "what is it," and once I had an answer I stopped looking, because the transaction was complete. Reed bunting. Tick. The morning it changed was in February of Year 11, and it was not dramatic. There was a heron at the pond, which was not a new bird, I had ticked heron in the first month. I had nothing to do because it was too cold and too early for anything else, so I just watched it, out of boredom, for about twenty-five minutes.

In twenty-five minutes it did not catch anything. It moved four times, each time a few steps, each time slower than I would have believed a living thing could move. Once it stopped mid-stride with a foot lifted and held it there for what I counted as fifty-one seconds. And at some point in there I understood that I had seen herons perhaps forty times and had never once seen a heron do anything, because I had always stopped watching at the moment of identification.

She said she had lived here for nineteen years assuming that whatever protections she had were extended to her by permission, and could be withdrawn the same way, and that learning the First Amendment was written down and applied to her had changed how she thought about her own job, where her manager had been shorting hours. In Year Ten I won the regional science fair with a project that was wrong.

Not wrong in a small way. The conclusion was wrong, the method was wrong, and the reason it won is that the presentation was excellent and I was very confident, and I have never fully got over how easy that turned out to be.

The project was on the water quality of the Ryhope Beck, which runs behind our estate and comes out near the old sewage works. The idea was to sample at five points along its length and show pollution increasing downstream of the industrial units on Coleman Road, which everyone locally assumes is the source. I bought a kit and tested for nitrate, phosphate, pH and dissolved oxygen. I made a poster with a map on it. My results showed exactly what I expected: readings got worse as you went downstream, with a big jump after Coleman Road.

Here is what I did wrong, and I did not find it out until the following spring.

I sampled all five sites on the same afternoon, in order, starting upstream at about two and finishing downstream at about half four. It is in fact the single thing you must not do, because the beck is affected by the treatment works discharge cycle, and it was a hot day in June, and dissolved oxygen falls through the afternoon as the water warms. So my downstream sites were not just downstream. They were later, and hotter, and I had built a beautiful graph in which the x-axis said distance and actually meant time of day.

I also had one sample per site. One. No repeats. A single reading from a moving body of water, which is roughly as meaningful as one photograph of a road reported as the traffic.

Nobody caught it. Not the judges, not my teacher, not the man from the water company. The only thing anyone asked me was why I had chosen the topic, and I said something about growing up next to it and caring about my community, which was true, and which they liked a lot.

What found the error was a boy called Aidan in the year above, who was not being kind. He said, at lunch, months later, that my graph would look the same if the beck was completely clean, because I had measured a day rather than a river. I was furious for about two hours and then I went home and looked at my times and felt the floor go.

I redid it that spring, properly. Three sites, sampled at the same time of day on nine different days, three replicates each, temperature recorded alongside every reading. It took eleven weeks instead of one afternoon, and the results were much less impressive. There is a real signal after Coleman Road, smaller than my first graph claimed, and a much bigger one after heavy rain everywhere, which turns out to be combined sewer overflow.

The thing I still think about is not that I was wrong. It is that I was wrong and rewarded, and that the reward came from the parts of the work that had nothing to do with whether it was true - the map, the confidence, the answer everybody in the room already believed about the industrial units.

I do not really trust myself when a result comes out the way I hoped. When my chemistry practical works first time I get suspicious rather than pleased, which I think is the most useful thing that fair gave me.

The certificate is still on the wall at my nan's. I have not had the conversation with her about it.

There were twenty-two dead laptops in a store room behind the physics lab, stacked like bricks, and for two years I walked past them almost every day. Most were the same model the government gave out in 2019. They all had stickers. He meant it as a joke, I think.

The first three were easy and made me stupid. One needed a RAM stick reseated. One had a dead CMOS battery. One had a charging port that had come off its pads, and I paid a man in the market forty rupees to re-solder it while I watched. Three working laptops went back to the school in a month, and I was, briefly, the boy who fixed the computers. I let people say it.

The other five did not go like that. Two would not post at all, and I decided the problem was the BIOS, because that is what a forum said about that model, and I flashed a chip using a programmer I had borrowed and a file I had not verified. I did it to both boards in the same evening, which is the single dumbest thing in this essay. If I had done one, waited, and seen it fail, I would have had one left. Instead I had two boards that were now genuinely dead instead of maybe dead, and a third that I cracked around the hinge trying to open it the wrong way.

I did not tell anyone for eleven days. When the vice-principal asked, I said the parts were not available, which was not a lie and was not the truth either. The project was stopped in December, politely, with the remaining laptops put back in the store room. I have to say that nobody was angry with me. That made it worse in a way I still cannot explain properly.

My father and I have not agreed about this for a year and a half. He repairs air conditioners and washing machines and he has done it since he was nineteen, so he has an opinion, and his opinion is that the mistake was doing the work for free. He says a man who is not paid is not allowed to say no, and cannot ask for time, and cannot say I do not know this one, bring it back Thursday. He is not wrong about the pressure. I did rush because I wanted to show three more before the term ended. But I think he is defending the wrong thing. I did not brick those boards because nobody paid me. I bricked them because I could not admit, out loud, in front of a teacher, that I had reached the end of what I knew. He says that is the same thing. I say it is not, and we go around like this, usually at the dinner table, usually with my mother telling us to eat.

What I did next was smaller than the story deserves. I bought a cheap logic probe and a multimeter and spent last summer at my father's workbench, not on laptops, on things he was already fixing, mostly holding the torch. I learned to write down the symptom before touching anything, and to change one variable, and to keep the old part in a bag with the date on it. In July I asked the school for four laptops again and this time I gave them a page saying what I could do, what I could not, and what I would do if I damaged one. Two are working. One is a screen I cannot afford. One I have not opened, and I am not going to until I know what is wrong with it.

My father still thinks I should charge. I still think that is not the lesson. He was the one who drove me to the school in July with the four laptops in the back of the scooter, so I know what he actually believes, whatever he says at dinner.

So the stretching became mine, not because anyone assigned it to me exactly, but because one morning I found Mia crying quietly at the kitchen table, unable to open a granola bar wrapper, and I sat down and did it for her, and then I stayed and did the stretches with her, and then I just kept showing up at 6:10 the next day, and the one after that.

It is not a complicated routine. I sit across from her, and we go through each finger, each knuckle, gently, while she tells me about whatever she's annoyed at that week - a friend, a teacher, a show she's behind on. It takes maybe fifteen minutes. Some mornings her hands are fine and we do it anyway, more out of habit than medical necessity, because by then it had become less about her joints and more about the fifteen minutes themselves, the only time in the day when it was just the two of us with nowhere to be yet.

I did not choose this the way I chose to join the debate team or sign up for AP Chemistry. It chose me, the way most of caregiving does, through absence - someone had to be there at 6:10, and I was the one who was. For a long time I resented that a little, quietly, the way you resent things you'd never say out loud because saying them makes you feel like a bad person. I wanted to sleep until 6:30 like everyone else I knew. I wanted mornings that were just mine.

What changed my mind about it wasn't a single moment so much as watching, slowly, what the fifteen minutes actually did. Mia started sleeping better, I think because she knew the mornings weren't going to ambush her anymore. I could tell from how she held a fork whether it was a stiff day. I could tell from her voice, half-asleep, whether she'd slept through the pain or fought it most of the night.

That skill - noticing the small stuff before it becomes the big stuff - is not something I learned in a classroom, and it's not something that shows up on a transcript.
